title: Yara and the Wardrobe
premise: Isandro Kavanagh, once the conservatory's most celebrated young pianist, returns two decades after a public breakdown ended his career — this time pushing a mop through the same corridors where he once performed. There he meets Yara Okonkwo-Bell, the last fluent speaker of Ilaro, a dying language her grandmother carried from a drowned coastal village, and she asks him to become her final student. As he learns the language, he discovers it holds no written record: every song, every name, every grievance of her people lives only in memory, including an old injustice committed by the conservatory itself against Yara's family. Learning Ilaro forces Isandro to confront the night he abandoned his own gift and betrayed a fellow student to protect his reputation. In the end, Isandro performs a forbidden piece in the conservatory's great hall — half requiem, half testimony — giving voice to both Yara's vanished village and his own buried guilt, while Yara, dying, passes the language on to a room of strangers who will carry fragments of it forward.
about_author: Odile Oyelaran is a former archivist who spent years cataloguing endangered sound recordings before turning to fiction. She writes about inheritance, silence, and the things institutions prefer to forget.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He begins work as a janitor at the Meridian Conservatory, moving invisibly through halls that once belonged to him. Students pass without recognizing him; one plays a piece he premiered at sixteen. The emotional beat is quiet estrangement — a man living inside his own erased life.

chapters.title: Water Sounds
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Cleaning the practice rooms at night, he hears an unfamiliar language spoken softly behind a locked door — rhythmic, tidal, nothing like the European repertoire around it. He lingers too long and is caught listening by an elderly woman with fierce eyes. The beat is intrusion into a sealed world.

chapters.title: Yara
chapters.summary: Yara's POV introduced. Ninety-one years old, she catalogs her memories aloud each evening because paper fails her now. She has buried three students' interest in learning Ilaro; all wanted a credential, none wanted the weight. She notices the janitor who listens at doors. The beat is solitary vigilance.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She tests Isandro unexpectedly, asking him to repeat a phrase of Ilaro. He does, imperfectly, and something in her decides. She offers him lessons — no fee, no certificate, no exit clause. Isandro, wary, accepts out of curiosity rather than commitment. The beat is a door opening.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Early lessons in Yara's cluttered apartment above a shuttered fish market. Ilaro has no word for 'finished,' only for 'carried.' Isandro finds the grammar strangely like music — tension, resolution, suspension. For the first time in years he wants something. The beat is reluctant hunger.

chapters.title: The Drowned Village
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She tells the story of Ilaro village, flooded for a reservoir in 1961, its residents dispersed, its dead moved but not consulted. Her grandmother sang the relocation hearings into memory — every broken promise preserved in song. The beat is grief held upright by discipline.

chapters.title: Repertoire
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. His daytime world intrudes: the conservatory plans a centennial gala, and staff are asked to contribute archival material. Isandro is assigned to the archive basement, where he finds recordings labeled with a name he knows — Adaeze Bell, Yara's mother, once a conservatory scholarship student. The beat is dread surfacing.

chapters.title: Adaeze
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Flashback woven through present-day lesson: her mother Adaeze won the conservatory's composition prize in 1958, then was stripped of it when the jury claimed her winning piece borrowed from 'folk material' — meaning her own heritage. The score was archived under a professor's name. The beat is inherited injustice, still warm.

chapters.title: What the Mop Knows
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He verifies the theft in the archive: correspondence, a altered manuscript, a career built on Adaeze's music by Professor Edmund Hale — whose name is carved on the concert hall. Isandro says nothing, but starts photographing documents. The beat is complicity turning toward action.

chapters.title: Suspension
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. A mid-book pivot inward: practicing Ilaro phrases, Isandro remembers his own collapse at twenty-two — the premiere he fled mid-performance, and how he let his rival take the blame for the sabotaged program that humiliated them both. Yara's language is loosening what he mopped over. The beat is memory rising like water.

chapters.title: No Word for Finished
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara's health declines; a stroke takes some English but leaves Ilaro untouched. Lessons shift to hospital rooms. She begins teaching Isandro the grievance songs — the ones meant to be sung publicly, at the wrongdoer's door. She is deciding something. The beat is urgency disguised as routine.

chapters.title: The Centennial Committee
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The gala committee wants 'heritage color': they invite Yara to sing an Ilaro blessing as decoration between acts. Isandro sees they intend to honor Hale's legacy the same night. He refuses to translate the invitation, buying time. The beat is the institution revealing itself.

chapters.title: Grievance Songs
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara explains the law outside law: in Ilaro tradition, a grievance song sung in the presence of the community binds the wrongdoer more tightly than any court — the debt becomes everyone's to witness. She asks Isandro whether he will help her sing Adaeze's case at the gala. The beat is a request that is also a test.

chapters.title: Hale's Heirs
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Isandro approaches the conservatory board quietly with the archive evidence and is met with procedural walls: statutes of limitation, reputational risk, an offer to 'honor Adaeze's influence' in a program note. He realizes justice will not be granted; it must be taken. The beat is institutional stonewalling hardening his resolve.

chapters.title: The Rival
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Isandro tracks down Tomas Reyes, the rival he betrayed decades ago, now a teacher in another city. The confrontation is raw: Tomas neither forgives nor refuses, but gives Isandro back the truth of that night in full detail. Isandro confesses to Yara afterward, in Ilaro, because the language has no soft evasions. The beat is confession as prerequisite.

chapters.title: Learning the Piece
chapters.summary: Dual POV alternating. Yara reconstructs Adaeze's stolen composition from memory — she heard her mother play it daily — while Isandro transcribes and relearns the piano, hands stiff, nerve unreliable. Practice scenes interleave with hospital vigils. The beat is two inheritances being rebuilt in parallel.

chapters.title: Permission
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The board, tipped off, threatens to bar Yara from the gala and have Isandro dismissed. Yara responds by recording the grievance songs and mailing copies to newspapers, descendants of the displaced villagers, and the Hale family. Justice stops being private. The beat is escalation — the quiet woman going loud.

chapters.title: Dress Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The night before the gala, Isandro rehearses alone in the empty hall and freezes at the same passage where his career ended. Yara, brought from the hospital against advice, sings him through it in Ilaro — the phrase means roughly 'the river does not apologize for arriving.' He plays past it. The beat is terror converted to momentum.

chapters.title: The Gala
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Mid-gala, after the tribute to Hale, Isandro walks onstage uninvited during the scheduled 'blessing' and instead performs Adaeze's restored composition, with Yara singing the grievance verses beside him. The hall erupts — half scandal, half standing ovation. The beat is the climax: testimony made undeniable in public.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Consequences arrive unevenly: an inquiry opens, Hale's name is not removed but a plaque to Adaeze is commissioned, scholarships renamed. It is not clean justice, and Isandro must accept partial repair. Tomas attends the plaque unveiling and stands beside him. The beat is justice as imperfect, witnessed settlement.

chapters.title: Carried
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara dies in early spring, mid-lesson, having finished — though Ilaro has no such word — the transfer of what she could give. At her funeral, the strangers she secretly taught over the years stand and speak fragments of Ilaro in turn, a chain she built without telling anyone. The beat is mourning braided with continuity.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, closing frame. A year later, Isandro teaches a small Saturday class of children in the old practice room, mop bucket still by the door because he kept the job. He is not the last speaker; he is one of several now. He plays Adaeze's piece as the students sing. The beat is inheritance fulfilled — ownership finally accepted.
